lesson_title: Paving the Corner: Completing the Square
hook_text: You're paving a yard. There's a hole in the corner. That hole is the whole method.
clip_script: You're paving a yard. Already down: a perfect square, x by x. Then you're given more paving — enough for six x more square metres — and you want the yard to end up square again. So you split it in half: two strips, three metres wide, one down the side, one along the bottom. Stand back. It's an L-shape. Almost a big square of side x plus three — except there's a hole in the corner. Exactly three by three. Nine square metres. Fill that hole and the yard is perfect. That's it. That's completing the square. Halve the middle number — six becomes three. Square it — three becomes nine. That's your corner tile. And if you're working with an equation, adding nine to one side means adding nine to the other, or the two sides stop being equal. So x squared plus six x equals minus two becomes x plus three, all squared, equals seven. Last step, and this is where people lose the mark: if a square is seven, the side could be root seven — or MINUS root seven. Plus or minus. Always. Two answers: minus three plus root seven, and minus three minus root seven.
visual_style: Overhead of a sunlit backyard: grey pavers forming a square, a delivery of extra pavers splitting into two strips, an L-shape with a glowing empty corner, then the corner tile dropping in and the whole square lighting up.
mood: Hands-on and satisfying, like a job finished properly.
pacing: Unhurried while the yard is built, a beat on the hole, crisp on the arithmetic.
